name: Guardian cryptic crossword, Penguin book 7 No 5

book.title: The New Penguin Book of The Guardian Crosswords, volume 7

clue.text: Try to obtain vessel for punch for swimmer’s home

blocks.note: to fish for something is to try to get it
punch is served from a punch bowl

explanation.surface: Someone hunting for a punch bowl that has been used as a home for a pet fish.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'swimmer' is a goldfish, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: A goldfish lives in a round glass tank, so the glass globe is where that pet spends its life.

clue.text: Composer’s to conduct, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is a spoken sound, so the word for conduct is taken by its sound only

blocks.note: to handle a matter is to conduct or manage it

explanation.surface: A remark that a composer is about to conduct his own music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conduct' tempts as musical conducting, but here it means manage or deal with.
explanation.definitionFit: George Frideric Handel, German-born Baroque musician who wrote Messiah, is a famous writer of music.

clue.text: Most primitive rites with ale circulating

indicators.note: something circulating moves round and about, so the letters are stirred into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Ancient ceremonies at which beer is passed round the circle of worshippers.
explanation.definitionFit: What came first in time, at the very beginning of development, is the least advanced or most primitive.

clue.text: Secondary routes familiar in East Anglia

blocks.note: first meaning: ..., the UK's minor numbered roads below A roads
second meaning: the Norfolk ..., shallow lakes and rivers of eastern England

explanation.walkthrough: In Britain, main roads are numbered A and lesser ones B. East Anglia is the eastern bulge of England, home to the Norfolk Broads waterways.
explanation.definitionFit: Read as B ROADS the word means minor highways; as one word it names the region's well-known lakes.

clue.text: Ma in three letters? Sh!

blocks.note: surface reading: how do you write a short word for mother with only three letters
setter's reading: the three-letter word for Ma is the answer to the riddle, and the whole phrase is also a call for silence

explanation.walkthrough: Mum is the British word for mother, and it also means silent, so the stock phrase does double duty.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying is an instruction to keep quiet and tell nobody, exactly what a whispered hush asks.

clue.text: Region incorrectly styled ‘La Mer’

indicators.note: something styled incorrectly is set out wrongly, so the letters need putting in a different order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A district wrongly named after Debussy's piece about the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A realm is a kingdom or domain, a territory or area of rule, so it can stand for a region.

clue.text: Duck a girl in the river to freshen up

indicators.note: something put in a river goes inside it, so the river's letters wrap around the others

blocks.note: a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, shaped like the letter O
a girl's name
the Dee is a river of Wales, England and Scotland

explanation.surface: Plunging a young woman into a river as a rough way of cleaning her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' looks like a verb meaning dunk, but it is the cricket zero.
explanation.definitionFit: Removing unpleasant smells from something is a way of making it smell clean and fresh again.

clue.text: Improver of texts, cryptic and remote

indicators.note: something cryptic is obscure and puzzling, hinting that these letters are disguised in a muddled order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Describing a textual editor as obscure and aloof.
explanation.definitionFit: One who emends corrects errors in written works, so a scholarly editor makes manuscripts better.

clue.text: Register a tenant? Not right at first

indicators.note: not having something means it is taken away from the word
at first points to the opening position as the place where the letter goes missing

blocks.note: a tenant pays rent
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A landlord wondering whether to sign up a tenant who is not quite suitable at first sight.
explanation.definitionFit: To enter details in a book or list is to record or register them formally.

clue.text: The nobility giving expensive rings

blocks.note: high prices are expensive ones
rings and circles are both round shapes

explanation.surface: Aristocrats handing out costly jewellery as presents.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes the top levels of society, where aristocrats and other people of rank mix.

clue.text: Most vigorous and tough — not half! — in case

indicators.note: not half means only part survives, so the back portion of that word is dropped

blocks.note: hard and tough both mean difficult or unyielding
lest means in case, for fear that

explanation.surface: Praising someone as fit and strong, with the jokey 'not half!' meaning 'and how!'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' is British slang for 'very much so', but here it literally halves the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Hale means healthy and robust, especially of an older person, so the superlative is the fittest or strongest.

clue.text: Pastoral cantata, on the subject of Nathaniel in the main

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so the earlier pieces go within the last

blocks.note: re means concerning or about
Nat is a short form of Nathaniel
the main is an old poetic term for the open ocean

explanation.surface: A country-style choral work about a man named Nathaniel at sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A serenata is an eighteenth-century dramatic cantata, often with pastoral subject matter, related to the serenade.

clue.text: Scolded, as judges are likely to be

definitions.text: as judges are likely to be
definitions.note: an adjective phrase: wearing a wig

blocks.note: first meaning: to wig someone is an old informal verb for telling them off

blocks.clueFragment: as judges are likely to be
blocks.note: second meaning: British judges traditionally wear horsehair wigs in court

explanation.walkthrough: In British courts judges and barristers still wear wigs; 'wigging' is a dated word for a scolding.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both the past tense of an old verb for reprimanding and an adjective for someone wearing a wig.

clue.text: A Swiss, ’e’s still, by way of example, withdrawn

indicators.note: withdrawn means pulled back, so the string of pieces is read backwards

blocks.note: 'e's is he's with the h dropped, leaving the letters ES
still and even both intensify, as in still better or even better
e.g. is the abbreviation for 'for example'

explanation.surface: A shy Swiss man described in Cockney speech as still holding back.
explanation.definitionFit: A Genevese is a native or inhabitant of Geneva, a city in Switzerland, so such a person is Swiss.

clue.text: Quick to catch a suitable dupe in place for cheap goods

indicators.note: to catch something is to hold it, so this word wraps around the following pieces

blocks.note: fleet means fast or quick
taken as written
a mark is a person picked out as easy to swindle

explanation.surface: A con artist hurrying to trap a gullible victim at a bargain stall.
explanation.definitionFit: An outdoor or street sale of second-hand items and bric-a-brac is a classic venue for bargains.

clue.text: Periodical going into society misdeeds and brawls

indicators.note: going into something means entering it, so this piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for society
crimes are misdeeds
a periodical is a magazine, shortened to mag

explanation.surface: A magazine exposing the bad behaviour and fights of high society.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrimmage is a confused struggle or scuffle, so the plural describes rough disorderly fights.

clue.text: Constructed, there’s only about one left

indicators.note: about means around, so one word goes round the pieces that follow

blocks.note: but can mean only, as in 'but a child'
I is the Roman numeral for one
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A builder noting that just about one item remains after the job is done.
explanation.definitionFit: Something built has been made or erected, the same past participle sense as put together.

clue.text: Mae’s final phase in London’s theatres?

definitions.note: plural in the clue, singular collective in the answer

blocks.note: Mae West was a Hollywood actress and stage star
the end is the final part
a stage is a phase of a process

explanation.surface: The last chapter of Mae West's career, played out on London stages.
explanation.walkthrough: The West End is London's main theatre district, like Broadway.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names professional theatre in central London's entertainment district collectively.

clue.text: Transport terminal with staff in one eastern capital

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the string formed by the following words

blocks.note: a means one
E is the abbreviation for eastern
Rome is the capital of Italy
a rod is a staff or stick

explanation.surface: A bus or air terminal with its workers posted in an eastern capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' tempts as employees, but it is a stick.
explanation.definitionFit: An aerodrome is an old word for an airfield, where passengers' journeys by plane begin and end.

clue.text: Useless ally, insensitive over defeat

blocks.note: dead to feeling means numb or insensitive
a loss is a defeat

explanation.surface: A partner who was useless and unfeeling about a defeat.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' means placed above, so the first piece comes before the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling a person this means they are of no help at all, a hopeless companion or partner.

clue.text: See 7
Commander scowls over me following a revolutionary decor

indicators.note: following means coming after, so the piece named before this word is placed second

blocks.note: CO is commanding officer
to lour is to frown or scowl
Che Guevara is the stock revolutionary
taken as written

explanation.surface: An officer frowning at me after a radical redecoration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' looks like an adjective for the decor but is the guerrilla Che Guevara.
explanation.definitionFit: The decor of a room is largely its chosen combination of paints, fabrics and hues.

clue.text: Said little, tipsy from an alcoholic product?

indicators.note: someone tipsy is unsteady and muddled, so these letters stagger into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who went quiet after too much drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the definition is loose: spirits are one kind of this product.
explanation.definitionFit: Spirits such as whisky are made by heating and condensing a fermented liquid, the process of distilling.

clue.text: Plant provides some playing-cards to relax

blocks.note: hearts are one of the four suits
to ease is to relax or loosen

explanation.surface: A card game offered as a way to unwind.
explanation.definitionFit: Heartsease is the wild pansy, a small European flower with purple and yellow petals.

clue.text: Ashamed, embarrassed, having most of meal rushed

indicators.note: someone embarrassed is flustered and thrown into confusion, so the letters are jumbled
most of a thing is all but a bit, so the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: taken as written
tea is an afternoon or evening meal in Britain

explanation.surface: A guest, red-faced, who bolted most of the food and hurried off.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain tea can be a light evening meal, not just a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: To make haste is an idiom for hurrying, so its past tense equals hurried or moved quickly.

clue.text: Former steward, settled in Yorkshire eventually

indicators.note: something settled in a place lives inside it, so the letters are lodged within the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the county name and the start of the next word

explanation.surface: A medieval estate manager who eventually made his home in the north of England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eventually' looks like a time word, but it only supplies letters. Yorkshire is a large county in northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: In medieval England a reeve was a manor's overseer or a local official acting for a lord or king.

clue.text: Get out of bed, as a chorus-girl will

definitions.note: a phrase describing an action, not a verb itself

blocks.note: first meaning: an old naval call to rise and get moving
second meaning: taken literally, a dancer in a high-kicking line displays her limbs

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase was a wake-up shout on sailing ships, where sleepers had to put a limb out of the hammock.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an idiomatic order to wake up and hurry, and literally what a high-kicking dancer does on stage.

clue.text: See 22
